body:
Gujarat's interest in verifiable government certificates

Government certificates are used to establish facts such as a person's educational qualification, income category, domicile or other recognised status. Their authenticity must often be checked when citizens apply for employment, education or public services.

On 25 April 2025, the Gujarat Administrative Reforms Commission (GARC) issued its Second Report. Under Reform 2.3, Verifiability of Government Certificates through Technology, it recommended making government-issued certificates, licences, clearances and similar documents verifiable through technology, particularly QR-code-based verification.

Its implementation guidelines also encouraged certificate-issuing departments to explore blockchain technology as an additional measure against fraudulent certificates and data-security problems.

The April 2025 GARC document makes a recommendation to explore blockchain. It does not, by itself, establish that a statewide blockchain certificate system was operational.

The report's discussion of encryption should not be read to mean that blockchain automatically encrypts every stored record. Confidentiality still depends on the specific security and access-control arrangements used.

QR-code verification and blockchain are different

A QR code is a machine-readable way of storing or linking to information. It can direct a verifier to an official certificate record. QR-code verification can work with an ordinary government database; blockchain is not a necessary condition.

In a blockchain-based verification arrangement, the QR code might help a user access a checking service, while the underlying shared ledger provides evidence about an authorised certificate record and its status. The QR code and blockchain would perform different functions.

Gujarat's e-Dhara land-record system

e-Dhara is a Government of Gujarat initiative for the computerisation and maintenance of village land records. Its documented functions include electronic records, processing of mutation applications and the issue of computerised Record of Rights (RoR) copies through e-Dhara centres.

Gujarat Informatics Limited describes the use of BhuLekh Soft for land-record workflows. This official description identifies e-Dhara as an electronic land-record system; it does not establish that e-Dhara is a blockchain implementation.

Digital land records are not automatically blockchain land records. A correct examination answer must distinguish a verified digital-government initiative from an assumed use of distributed ledger technology.

Putting the main concepts together

The core ideas of blockchain are connected but distinct. A distributed ledger lets multiple participants maintain records under common rules. A blockchain organises records in cryptographically linked blocks. Consensus determines the accepted history. Immutability makes later tampering difficult and detectable. Smart contracts execute predefined rules. Governance determines participation, responsibility, corrections and changes to the system.

Each property answers a different question. Consensus addresses agreement, immutability addresses alteration, smart contracts address rule-based execution and governance addresses institutional control.

The limits remain important

A shared record is useful only when the underlying information is reliable. Blockchain cannot independently prove that a medicine is genuine, that a certificate was properly awarded or that a land claimant has lawful ownership. It also cannot replace the responsible public authority where the law requires an official decision.

In a well-designed public-service system, blockchain can support record integrity and verification, while authorised officials, legal procedures, privacy controls and ordinary institutional accountability continue to perform their necessary roles.

Prelims focus

  • GARC's Second Report is dated 25 April 2025.
  • Reform 2.3 concerns technological verification of government certificates.
  • GARC encouraged departments to explore blockchain; this was not proof of statewide deployment.
  • QR-code verification can operate without blockchain.
  • e-Dhara is a documented electronic land-record initiative using BhuLekh Soft.
  • Trap: A government recommendation, a proof of concept and a fully operating statewide system are 3 different implementation statuses.

[Gujarat Administrative Reforms Commission, Second Report of GARC, 25 April 2025, Reform 2.3, pp. 19–21, particularly Section 5.1, p. 20; Gujarat Informatics Limited, e-Dhara – Land Records Online, Project Description and Objectives, consulted 5 November 2026; District Surat, Government of Gujarat, E-Dhara Land Records, consulted 5 November 2026; NIST, Blockchain, overview, consulted 5 November 2026; UK National Cyber Security Centre, Distributed Ledger Technology, Distributed Ledger Technology section, consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Certificate verification may use a QR code without requiring the underlying record system to be a blockchain.

pictures.alt: Six questions distinguish the roles of distributed ledger, blockchain, consensus, immutability, smart contracts and governance, while highlighting the need for trustworthy inputs.
pictures.caption: Blockchain combines shared records, consensus, tamper resistance, executable rules and governance.

title: Blockchain in Gujarat: Verified Context and Final Prelims Revision
